Title: Comment from NELDA LYCKA
comment_text: I am requesting that a permit to build a crude oil tank farm near my home be DENIED. As a homeowner of 42 years on County Road 304 (Peach Point Road) and a resident of Jones Creek, Texas, for nearly 60 years, I want to state that I am OPPOSED to a tank farm being built near my house. We have significant problems with flooding in this area and a project like this will worsen those issues. This project will disrupt the lives of myself and my neighbors with truck traffic on our narrow country road, cause danger to persons and wildlife, impact the already fragile drainage of the area, and create unwanted nighttime light pollution and noise in our rural residential neighborhood. I DO NOT WANT A TANK FARM WITHIN SIGHT OF MY HOUSE. The proposed project by Texas GulfLink/Sentinel Midstream on CR 304 should be STOPPED. Other property is available that will not disrupt the lives of people in Jones Creek. GulfLink has only been in business one year and has never completed such a project. I am asking MARAD to please DENY this permit. Nelda Lycka 202 Peach Point Jones Creek, TX 77541

Title: Comment from Annette Hardesty
comment_text: The announcement of the possible location for this oil tank farm on CR 304 in Jones Creek is some of the most unbelievable and shocking information anyone could possibly receive! We purchased this property many years ago, and built our home here with the belief that we were selecting a place that would be peaceful and quiet. We would be away from the hustle and bustle associated with the industrial areas.... and commercial, industrial plants, farms, etc! It would be a pleasant location OUT IN THE COUNTRY! We would never have suspected we would have Oil Storage Tanks BASICALLY in our front yards! I would like to ask if ANYONE (especially the representatives from Sentinel) would be happy or excited to have this located right in front of their homes?? I cannot believe the answer would be YES! Next comes all the NORMAL questions!! (These are only a few... and Im sure there are many people with more advanced questions that need to be addressed) What about drainage... which, if not handled properly could definitely result in flooding issues? (Weve had BROKEN promises for YEARS from the county about this... so I suppose more lies really wouldnt be a shock! What about the obvious... many, many environmental issues? Are there ANY possibilities of leaks or ANYTHING to contaminate ground water? Just in case no one is aware... there are 4 homes (one of these is my home) that is in the IMMEDIATE area ... just across the street from the proposed location! Our water supply is from our own water wells... and this is a definite cause for concern! What about dangers from air quality control (fumes), fires, explosions, etc? Again, this is right across the street from our homes! I can only imagine what this will do for the value of our homes and property. There is no way we will ever be able to sell them. (That is, other than possibly to another industrial site!) No family would desire to live with an oil storage tank farm across the street!! (Well, maybe so.... but that would only be the Judas that is selling out to pad his own pockets and cares for no one else!) Also, on a smaller scale, what is planned for the control of the feral hogs and other wildlife that has been driven out of their habitats into OUR yards? Obviously, more areas are going to be cleared out.... only eliminating more of their natural areas! The destruction is horrible and unbelievable... but they have nowhere to go! This is only a point of information, and a minor thing considering all the other problems associated with this proposed location! Yes, I am UPSET I am ANGRY I am HURT But most of all, I am TERRIFIED of the possible problems! I have worked very hard to provide a home for myself, my children, and my grandchildren! I have also worked very hard to try to keep it presentable AND NEVER intended it to become part of an industrial site with industrial problems!!!! We ARE NOT welcoming you with open arms!! Please reconsider and move this to a more suitable location!! Annette Hardesty-Brown Peach Point Rd - CR 304 Jones Creek, TX

Title: Comment from Nicole Hardesty
comment_text: I am a homeowner in the Village of Jones Creek, Texas. Texas GulfLink, LLC, a newly formed company of just one year, is proposing a tank farm be build on the outskirts of our Village. This would have devastating affects on the residents in my community. Tank farms are inherently dangerous. According to a study published in The Journal of Loss Prevention in Process Industries, of 242 accidents that occurred over a 40 year period, 30% were due to human error. 33% were due to lightning strikes. Several other causes were named; equipment failure and sabotage were just a few of them. These causes cannot be controlled; therefore, this or any tank farm should not be built in a residential area. Water displacement is the major concern for us. We rely on natural drainage in Jones Creek. The footprint that this facility will take up will limit the amount of water that can be absorbed back into the earth. The amount of water that the proposed six foot levee will displace, should a flood occur, would cause significant damage to homes in our community. Our drainage is already compromised in this area. We cannot have more water displaced on us. Noise and light pollution are another concern. The property they wish to build on is a country road. It will completely change the landscape and view for homeowners across the street and beyond. The impact construction and operation on our roads is something we cannot handle. As well as not having the city services or infrastructure to support industry of this kind. There are many more suitable properties available to this company that will not impact the residents like this one will. I urge you all to DENY their permits and make them move to an area more suited for industry to this size.

This community at fair great risk of devastation from flooding, property devaluation,worsening of already heavily traveled small county roads from other construction site, lack of any Emergency medical and fire to contain any disaster that could happen, and what the residents of this community perceive as a major negative impact to not only out homes, but safety as well. Those that have homes across the street from the proposed site, feel that not only does this decrease the value of their homes, but who wants to look out the window at such a monstrosity, or the light pollution, likely hood of more flooding, being able to leave their homes or even walk across the road to their mailboxes because of the ridiculous amount of traffic this will impose on this small county road???? Title: Comment from Deborah and Tom Williamson
comment_text: The first reason is that we did not move to a rural area expecting to have it industrialized by an oil tank farm. Building this tank farm will ruin our rural roads, not to mention an increase in traffic and traffic-related problems. Thirteen huge tanks, across from a residential area will consume beautiful pasture land and displace cattle and wildlife. It will require the building of a massive power plant and 3 huge observation towers, as well. The light, noise, and land pollution will have an immense impact. It will also require miles of pipeline, as we are 28.3 nautical miles from where the oil is to be pumped. Ground will be torn up throughout the entire village while laying these pipelines. Our second reason is that we are an historic site. Jones Creek is where Stephen F. Austin brought the original 300 colonists to settle land, bought from Mexico, before Texas was a Republic. This is where he wrote the Texas Constitution. An historic church still stands in our village and its graveyard is where he was originally buried before being exhumed and moved to the capital in Austin. The proposed tank farm would be located less than a mile from this historic site. Next, we have a wildlife preserve located less than 2 miles from the proposed tank farm site. We are also a bird sanctuary. Disruption of deer, birds, horses, cattle and other wildlife will be impacted by the building of this industrial oil tank storage facility. Our community was hit hard by Hurricane Harvey. We have many low-lying areas prone to flooding when we receive 8 inches of rainfall in a short period of time. Building a tank farm would displace water and cause massive flooding in our village. Should the Brazos River flood quickly, pipelines can come off the ground, float, break and cause seepage. This project is proposing a 6 ft. levee around 200 acres. That would be 325,851 X 6 ft. = 65,170,200 gallons. Then, 65,170,200 X 200 acres = 391,021,200 gallons! That would be the maximum amount of water displaced from a rising water event. This number does not take into account the slope of the levee. Building this tank farm will flood the homes of residents who made this area their home long before any unwanted industrialization was conceived. Another primary concern is that this tank farm will be less than 2 miles from our elementary school. Pipeline construction will tear up roads making it dangerous for children to ride their bikes or walk to school, not to mention an extreme increase in other traffic situations. Star-gazing observations for science classes will no longer be possible due to light pollution from the proposed tank farm facility. (Weve never heard of building an oil storage tank farm this close to a public school full of children). Our final reason for not wanting a tank farm in our rural residential neighborhood is the dangers of tank farms themselves. Neither of these tank farms are near available water sources since residents are all on wells. In the event of a tank fire, there would be no available water in the area for them to use to put the fire out. The Simon Fraser University Report of 2004 states that 242 tank farm accidents occurred over a 40 year period with 33% due to lightning, 30% human error, and 37% mechanical and equipment failure. This report stated that explosions are not uncommon, plus cracks in tanks, static electricity problems, open flames, ruptures, and engineering incompetence. For this reason most tank farms are located in remote or industrial areas. Fallout for our community could involve explosions, wildfires, air pollution due to chemical particulates, wildlife and human loss of life, and other damage to the environment. In conclusion, we do not feel a 13 tank storage farm is safe for our village of Jones Creek. It would pose a blight on the beauty of our community as well as a danger to our residents and school children. It would threaten our wildlife preserve, bird sanctuary, livestock and crops. Our groundwater could easily be contaminated by pipeline leaks and our wells would be ruined. Air, noise and light pollution will occur. Toxic fumes are an inevitability. Flooding will become a major issue and it could negatively impact our historic sites. It would be bad for the environment and could cause a myriad of health issues. It is an injustice that industry does not consider the dangerous consequences of tank farms in residential areas, only giving consideration to capacity and monetary gain. Please consider these facts and concerns of our tiny village. We need you to look out for our rights over industrys wants. Look into your hearts and ask yourselves would you want this in your neighborhood near your childrens school? Our county already has a disproportionate amount of industry; we dont need tank farms in our village! Tom and Deborah Williamson

Title: Comment from Justin Wright
comment_text: To whom it may concern: I am writing this public response as a concerned Village of Jones Creek resident who greatly opposes the currently proposed location of this bulk storage facility. The proposed location will undoubtedly impose intolerable adversities and risks to our Village residents, their homes, our local infrastructure (i.e. country roads not designed for construction loads and traffic), and Federally protected wildlife. Additionally, the tank farm would impose nuisance odors and illumination pollution to residential homes in close proximity. This bulk storage facility would adversely impact and without regard, the country lifestyle/aesthetics our residents (many of whom are retired and infeasible to relocate) have worked their entire life to achieve. The proposed location is in a flooding-prone area that will displace water on residential property/homes and roads that already experience common flooding issues. The small country roads required to mobilize heavy construction equipment and materials would deteriorate quickly under such usage. It has also been a known and proven fact that the proposed location would destroy the home of bald eagles that represent America and the American spirit within our Village residents. The increased traffic will (undeniably through traffic study and statistics) increase the amount of motor vehicle accidents in our area, and again the roads were not designed with such intent. It is not by chance and without merit and just cause, that Texas State Representative, Dennis Bonnen, County Commissioner, David Linder, Jones Creek Marshall, William Tidwell, Jones Creek City Council Representatives, and voluminous amounts of Jones Creek residents have publicly taken a stand against the location of this project. This project is better suited for another location with adequate infrastructure to support it, and would be an irresponsible and deplorable example of placing capitalism over people, safety, and conservation. Regards, Justin R. Wright

Title: Comment from John Simmons
comment_text: Texas Gulflinks proposed deep water port project includes an onshore tank farm. The site the they have selected for the tank farm will put many existing residents and their properties in unnecessary danger. In 2006 a study on tank farm accidents was published in the Journal for Loss Prevention in Process Industries. The purpose of the paper was to understand the causes that led to 242 worldwide tank accidents that occurred over a 40-year period. 33% of those accidents were caused by lightening. Another 30% were caused by human error. Other causes were equipment failure and sabotage. None of these causes can be fully controlled. In my opinion, not the kind of installation reasonable people would put near an existing residential community. Tank farms are dangerous. They catch fire. They explode. People get hurt. Property is destroyed. Texas GulfLink wants to build a tank farm inside of a rural community called Jones Creek Community. Please note that the Jones Creek Community extends considerably beyond the boundaries established by The Village of Jones Creek. A large number of people who reside outside of the village boundaries consider themselves members of the Jones Creek Community, as demonstrated by our growing petition against this project. The tank farm issue is a concern of the vast majority of the Jones Creek Community members. Tank farms are dangerous and should not be built in the midst of established residential communities. Industrial developments such as this that push into the midst a residential community such as ours brings dangerous and unpleasant circumstances to the already established community. Other credible issues that will have impact on the community is drainage, noise pollution, light pollution, air pollution, road destruction, residential property devaluation, traffic, especially during the construction phase. There are other suitable sites available for this project that do not impact residential developments. Please, give serious consideration to these issues and reject Texas GulfLinks permit for this project in its current form. Just because there is no prohibitive law or statute for certain activities doesnt mean its a good idea. Sometimes were called upon to use our common sense.

Title: Comment from Nelda Lycka
comment_text: Before you approve the location of the tank farm for this project in Jones Creek, Texas, you should study Texas history. This area is the "Cradle of Texas." Stephen F. Austin, the "Father of Texas" and his family originally located here at Peach Point Plantation. Historic cemeteries, churches, buildings, and historical markers set this area apart from all others. The very founding of Texas occurred here, the first capital of Texas was located in West Columbia, the historic Battle of Velasco during the Texas Revolution happened nearby, and the detention of Mexican General Santa Anna at the Varner-Hogg Plantation site after his defeat and capture at San Jacinto. Less than a mile from the proposed tank farm is the original burial site of Stephen F. Austin. This IS NOT an appropriate place to put an industrial crude oil tank farm. Please take the extensive history of our area in mind and DO NOT approve the application for Texas GulfLink to place a tank farm here.

Title: Comment from Donna Hoffman
comment_text: I am an American and I implore you to deny the MARAD-2019-0093 Deepwater Port License Application: Texas GulfLink LLC. Title: Comment from Mary Wildfire
comment_text: I wish to object to the licensing of the GulfLink Export facility. I understand there is a long list of issues involving water and air pollution and endangerment of the ecosystems and therefore fishing and tourism; but I will leave such matters to others because I live in West Virginia. This however is on the very same planet as this proposed facility, and therefore I am concerned about the impact on the climate of building a NEW facility to store and export oil--at a time when we should be working hard to phase out oil use. The Earth and its ecosystems cannot endure further climate chaos. This is not some wild theory but the consensus opinion of climate science. The fact that oil companies, pipeline companies and related companies have profits or financial viability at stake should not trump the fact that our children and grandchildren have physical survival at stake. Money creates great political pressure in our system but it should not drive us to accepting extinction, or seeing human wellbeing as a secondary matter. Yes, I am also making these points in connection with the many proposals for giant pipelines and petrochemical facilities in my own backyard. Some impacts are local but continuing to push for expansion, or business-as-usual for fossil fuels at this late date is criminally irresponsible, An extreme statement? Only if you think protecting human life is unimportant and prioritizing it is extreme.

Title: Comment from Sophie Shemas
comment_text: I am writing to express opposition to Texas GulfLink LLC's application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration, and raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review (DEIS). First and foremost, I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while placing massive burdens on local communities, the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and the global climate. This project therefore is not in the "national interest." I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of a major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. It has been ten years since the Deepwater Horizon disaster that decimated our Gulf Coast - our marine ecosystems and coastal communities are still struggling to recover and can't afford another disaster. The DEIS does not adequately analyze oil spill risks, especially potential impacts on the endangered Black Rail and critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle. Impacts from air pollution emissions associated with this project are also of deep concern. Local residents cannot afford the additional pollution burdens, as the region is already classified as nonattainment for EPA's health-based air quality standards for ozone, and NOx emissions would also exceed the threshold for concern. I am alarmed that the EIS does not consider the very real and foreseeable direct and indirect impacts of the project's greenhouse gas emissions on climate change. 2020 was a record storm season for the Gulf, battering many communities with flooding from storm surges. It is widely understood that crude exports are driving the rapid increase of oil and gas drilling in the Permian Basin - oil that could otherwise be left in the ground. MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. The Texas coastline is eroding at an average rate of 2 to 10 feet per year, and Freeport is experiencing sea level rise at a rate of 17 inches per 100 years. It is in this context that MARAD must evaluate the environmental justice impacts of the proposed GulfLink project. Given all of these impacts and inadequacies, I urge MARAD to deny the Deepwater Port License Application for the Texas GulfLink. The project is not in the national interest and imposes too many risks and burdens on our Gulf Coast communities and ecosystems.

Title: Comment from Louise Slattery
comment_text: I would like to express opposition to the Texas GulfLink LLC application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers, raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review, and request a public hearing on the USACE permitting process due to the extreme risks the project presents to all communities including flooding, contamination of our water supply, the Brazos Watershed, and Gulf Waters. I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while polluting local communities and the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and escalating the global climate crisis. Brazoria County is home to some of the state's most precious natural resources. Beyond their intrinsic natural beauty, healthy beaches and wetlands provide effective storm damage and flood protection; offer residents and visitors recreational opportunities; and provide unique environmental habitats. When the GulfLink pipeline ruptures it will contaminate the Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area, a rich, bio-diverse wetland wildlife sanctuary prized for waterfowl hunting. The coastal region is an economic engine filled with recreational opportunities and environmental treasures that deserve to be protected. I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of another major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. Gulf marine life has suffered tremendously from the Deepwater Horizon spill, killing sea turtles and nearly destroying the dolphin population. Oil, gas, and chemical infrastructure dominate the Gulf and leak toxic chemicals and oil, contaminating waters every year. In 2018, NOAA reported 137 significant" oil spills in the U.S., most of them occurring in the Gulf of Mexico, making the recovery of endangered species including the Kemp's ridley sea turtle a long, difficult process. Oil toxins remain in over 2,500 sampled fish from over 300 Gulf locations according to the National Wildlife Federation.

Brazoria County is home to some of the state's most precious natural resources. Beyond their intrinsic natural beauty, our healthy beaches and wetlands provide effective storm damage and flood protection; offer residents and visitors recreational opportunities; and provide unique environmental habitats. When the GulfLink pipeline ruptures it will contaminate the Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area, a rich, bio-diverse wetland wildlife sanctuary prized for waterfowl hunting. Our coastal region is an economic engine filled with recreational opportunities and environmental treasures that deserve to be protected. I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of another major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. Our Gulf marine life has suffered tremendously from the Deepwater Horizon spill, killing sea turtles and nearly destroying the dolphin population. Oil, gas, and chemical infrastructure dominate the Gulf and leak toxic chemicals and oil, contaminating our waters every year. In 2018, NOAA reported 137 significant" oil spills in the U.S., most of them occurring in the Gulf of Mexico, making the recovery of endangered species including the Kemp's ridley sea turtle a long, difficult process. Oil toxins remain in over 2,500 sampled fish from over 300 Gulf locations according to the National Wildlife Federation.

I would like to express opposition to the Texas GulfLink LLC application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers, raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review, and request a public hearing on the USACE permitting process due to the extreme risks the project presents to our communities including flooding, contamination of our water supply, the Brazos Watershed, and Gulf Waters. I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while polluting local communities and the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and escalating the global climate crisis. Brazoria County is home to some of the state's most precious natural resources. Beyond their intrinsic natural beauty, our healthy beaches and wetlands provide effective storm damage and flood protection; offer residents and visitors recreational opportunities; and provide unique environmental habitats. When the GulfLink pipeline ruptures it will contaminate the Justin Hurst Wildlife Management Area, a rich, bio-diverse wetland wildlife sanctuary prized for waterfowl hunting. Our coastal region is an economic engine filled with recreational opportunities and environmental treasures that deserve to be protected. I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of another major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. Our Gulf marine life has suffered tremendously from the Deepwater Horizon spill, killing sea turtles and nearly destroying the dolphin population. Oil, gas, and chemical infrastructure dominate the Gulf and leak toxic chemicals and oil, contaminating our waters every year. In 2018, NOAA reported 137 significant" oil spills in the U.S., most of them occurring in the Gulf of Mexico, making the recovery of endangered species including the Kemp's ridley sea turtle a long, difficult process. Oil toxins remain in over 2,500 sampled fish from over 300 Gulf locations according to the National Wildlife Federation.
topics_str: Oil spill risk, Marine wildlife, Wetlands & coast

comment_text: I would like to express opposition to the Texas GulfLink LLC application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers, raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review, and request a public hearing on the USACE permitting process due to the extreme risks the project presents to our communities including flooding, contamination of our water supply, the Brazos Watershed, and Gulf Waters. Our coastal region is an economic engine filled with recreational opportunities and environmental treasures that deserve to be protected. In 2018, NOAA reported 137 significant" oil spills in the U.S., most of them occurring in the Gulf of Mexico, making the recovery of endangered species including the Kemp's ridley sea turtle a long, difficult process. Oil toxins remain in over 2,500 sampled fish from over 300 Gulf locations according to the National Wildlife Federation. Our communities depend on both the commercial and sport fishing industries. Title: Comment from Bonnie Barfield
comment_text: I am writing to express opposition to Texas GulfLink LLC's application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration, and raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review (DEIS). First and foremost, I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while placing massive burdens on local communities, the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and the global climate. This project therefore is not in the "national interest." I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of a major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. It has been ten years since the Deepwater Horizon disaster that decimated our Gulf Coast - our marine ecosystems and coastal communities are still struggling to recover and can't afford another disaster. The DEIS does not adequately analyze oil spill risks, especially potential impacts on the endangered Black Rail and critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle. Impacts from air pollution emissions associated with this project are also of deep concern. Local residents cannot afford the additional pollution burdens, as the region is already classified as nonattainment for EPA's health-based air quality standards for ozone, and NOx emissions would also exceed the threshold for concern. I am alarmed that the EIS does not consider the very real and foreseeable direct and indirect impacts of the project's greenhouse gas emissions on climate change. 2020 was a record storm season for the Gulf, battering many communities with flooding from storm surges. It is widely understood that crude exports are driving the rapid increase of oil and gas drilling in the Permian Basin - oil that could otherwise be left in the ground. MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. The Texas coastline is eroding at an average rate of 2 to 10 feet per year, and Freeport is experiencing sea level rise at a rate of 17 inches per 100 years. It is in this context that MARAD must evaluate the environmental justice impacts of the proposed GulfLink project. Given all of these impacts and inadequacies, I urge President Biden and MARAD to deny the Deepwater Port License Application for the Texas GulfLink. President Biden promised to take bold action to challenge the fossil fuel industry and reign in US greenhouse gas emissions. Permitting crude export infrastructure will only exacerbate climate pollution, and is antithetical to sound climate policy. The project is not in the national interest and imposes too many risks and burdens on our Gulf Coast communities and ecosystems.

MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. First and foremost, I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while placing massive burdens on local communities, the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and the global climate. This project therefore is not in the "national interest." I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of a major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. It has been ten years since the Deepwater Horizon disaster that decimated our Gulf Coast - our marine ecosystems and coastal communities are still struggling to recover and can't afford another disaster. The DEIS does not adequately analyze oil spill risks, especially potential impacts on the endangered Black Rail and critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle. Impacts from air pollution emissions associated with this project are also of deep concern. Local residents cannot afford the additional pollution burdens, as the region is already classified as nonattainment for EPA's health-based air quality standards for ozone, and NOx emissions would also exceed the threshold for concern. I am alarmed that the EIS does not consider the very real and foreseeable direct and indirect impacts of the project's greenhouse gas emissions on climate change. 2020 was a record storm season for the Gulf, battering many communities with flooding from storm surges. It is widely understood that crude exports are driving the rapid increase of oil and gas drilling in the Permian Basin - oil that could otherwise be left in the ground. MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. The Texas coastline is eroding at an average rate of 2 to 10 feet per year, and Freeport is experiencing sea level rise at a rate of 17 inches per 100 years. It is in this context that MARAD must evaluate the environmental justice impacts of the proposed GulfLink project. Given all of these impacts and inadequacies, I urge President Biden and MARAD to deny the Deepwater Port License Application for the Texas GulfLink. President Biden promised to take bold action to challenge the fossil fuel industry and reign in US greenhouse gas emissions. Permitting crude export infrastructure will only exacerbate climate pollution, and is antithetical to sound climate policy. The project is not in the national interest and imposes too many risks and burdens on our Gulf Coast communities and ecosystems.

Title: Comment from B. Ann
comment_text: I support Texas GulfLink, and as an environmentalist, wildlife enthusiast, and Gulf Coast resident for over 30 years, urge MARAD and EPA to approve this project. Texas GulfLink will play a role in the global shift from sulphur-based fuels to more environmentally friendly fuels refined by sweet crude. Texas is well positioned as a leader in producing sweet crude (i.e. WTI), which can now be exported to developing economies all over the world. No longer are these countries disenfranchised with a lack of access to affordable, sweet crude. This is global environmental justice at work. Sulphur is an undesirable characteristic of petroleum products, particularly in transportation fuels, and requires more severe processing to remove the sulphur.. It can hinder the efficient operation of some emission control technologies and, when burned in a combustion engine, is released into the atmosphere where it can form sulphur dioxide. With increasingly restrictive sulphur limits on transportation fuels, sweet crude is needed worldwide. Texas GulfLink will be able to load this sweet crude on tankers, safer and more efficient than current methods. If we are to battle climate change, it must start in steps, and one of those steps is the removal of Sulphur from bunker fuels, a movement known as IMO 2020. Developing nations need access to affordable fossil fuel. Developing nations cannot progress without energy - We cannot ignore our neighbors on this planet, our home is home to all. Lastly, several miles away from the coast, hundreds of ships each year load crude oil, creating more emissions than what is a proposed by a deepwater port. These ports will reduce the current operation, and vastly improve our air quality by eliminating emissions that are here today. Yes there will be emissions, but it will be LESS than the no action alternative. We're talking about removing thousands of tons per year of VOC. This is great!! - If people are passionate about health affects, what luxury to attack oil and gas and not fast food or VOC direct contacts through grease cooking? I never understand the focus, but that is the freedom of speech our great country allows. The government should know that many of the commenters on this project are outsiders from other states that do not understand the regional and global positive impact a project like this would have, they DO NOT speak for us. These groups continue to reach out to our community and use unprofessional tactics through social media and harassment of supporters. I hope there is civility in the difference of opinion. The oil and gas industry spends millions of dollars being environmental stewards, and going above and beyond what normal citizens would do to our lands. Positive for the global fight against climate change, positive for economic development, and positive for protecting our coast from ship congestion and accident probability.

Title: Comment from Raquel Buxton
comment_text: I am writing to express opposition to Texas GulfLink LLC's application for a Deepwater Port License from the Maritime Administration, and raise concerns with significant inadequacies in the project's environmental review (DEIS). First and foremost, I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while placing massive burdens on local communities, the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and the global climate. This project therefore is not in the "national interest." I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of a major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. It has been ten years since the Deepwater Horizon disaster that decimated our Gulf Coast - our marine ecosystems and coastal communities are still struggling to recover and can't afford another disaster. The DEIS does not adequately analyze oil spill risks, especially potential impacts on the endangered Black Rail and critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle. Impacts from air pollution emissions associated with this project are also of deep concern. Local residents cannot afford the additional pollution burdens, as the region is already classified as nonattainment for EPA's health-based air quality standards for ozone, and NOx emissions would also exceed the threshold for concern. I am alarmed that the EIS does not consider the very real and foreseeable direct and indirect impacts of the project's greenhouse gas emissions on climate change. 2020 was a record storm season for the Gulf, battering many communities with flooding from storm surges. It is widely understood that crude exports are driving the rapid increase of oil and gas drilling in the Permian Basin - oil that could otherwise be left in the ground. MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. The Texas coastline is eroding at an average rate of 2 to 10 feet per year, and Freeport is experiencing sea level rise at a rate of 17 inches per 100 years. It is in this context that MARAD must evaluate the environmental justice impacts of the proposed GulfLink project. Given all of these impacts and inadequacies, I urge President Biden and MARAD to deny the Deepwater Port License Application for the Texas GulfLink. President Biden promised to take bold action to challenge the fossil fuel industry and reign in US greenhouse gas emissions. Permitting crude export infrastructure will only exacerbate climate pollution, and is antithetical to sound climate policy. The project is not in the national interest and imposes too many risks and burdens on our Gulf Coast communities and ecosystems.

First and foremost, I am concerned that construction and operation of the export facility would only benefit oil and gas industry interests while placing massive burdens on local communities, the Gulf of Mexico's coastal and marine ecosystems, and the global climate. This project therefore is not in the "national interest." I am deeply concerned about potentially catastrophic impacts of a major oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico. It has been ten years since the Deepwater Horizon disaster that decimated our Gulf Coast - our marine ecosystems and coastal communities are still struggling to recover and can't afford another disaster. The DEIS does not adequately analyze oil spill risks, especially potential impacts on the endangered Black Rail and critically endangered Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle. Impacts from air pollution emissions associated with this project are also of deep concern. Local residents cannot afford the additional pollution burdens, as the region is already classified as nonattainment for EPA's health-based air quality standards for ozone, and NOx emissions would also exceed the threshold for concern. I am alarmed that the EIS does not consider the very real and foreseeable direct and indirect impacts of the project's greenhouse gas emissions on climate change. 2020 was a record storm season for the Gulf, battering many communities with flooding from storm surges. It is widely understood that crude exports are driving the rapid increase of oil and gas drilling in the Permian Basin - oil that could otherwise be left in the ground. MARAD must analyze the full lifecycle climate impacts of oil drilling, transportation, refining, and consumption that would result from this project. Finally, I am concerned that the EIS does not consider environmental justice impacts. Toxic pollution from existing oil and gas infrastructure disproportionately burdens low-income, minority communities in the Gulf of Mexico region. And, these communities are at ground zero for the impacts of climate change, including sea level rise, increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, and loss of critically protective wetlands. The Texas coastline is eroding at an average rate of 2 to 10 feet per year, and Freeport is experiencing sea level rise at a rate of 17 inches per 100 years. It is in this context that MARAD must evaluate the environmental justice impacts of the proposed GulfLink project. Given all of these impacts and inadequacies, I urge President Biden and MARAD to deny the Deepwater Port License Application for the Texas GulfLink. President Biden promised to take bold action to challenge the fossil fuel industry and reign in US greenhouse gas emissions. Permitting crude export infrastructure will only exacerbate climate pollution, and is antithetical to sound climate policy. The project is not in the national interest and imposes too many risks and burdens on our Gulf Coast communities and ecosystems.
